name: Quiptic crossword No 1,154
preamble: 28/12/2021 Clue for 12 across has been corrected

clue.text: Reveal end of world is not far away

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: the closing letter of the word
taken as written
close means near at hand

explanation.surface: An apocalyptic warning: someone revealing that the world's end is near.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads as a doom-laden announcement, but 'end of world' only supplies a single letter and 'not far away' is a plain synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: To reveal a secret is to make it known, a direct verb synonym with matching tense.

clue.text: Late decree — ordered to slow down

indicators.note: putting things in order means rearranging them, so the letters are set out afresh

blocks.note: the ten letters used as raw material

explanation.surface: A last-minute government decree imposing a speed restriction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ordered' looks like part of the decree story, as in a ruling being issued, but it signals a rearrangement of the two words before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Decelerate is the technical verb for reducing speed, the exact opposite of accelerate.

clue.text: Gives a brief account of tot with mum on hikes?

blocks.note: a tot is an addition, as in totting up figures
an informal word for mother
price hikes are rises

explanation.surface: A report on a toddler and its mother out walking in the hills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tot' suggests a small child and 'hikes' suggests walks, but tot is a sum to be added up and hikes are increases.
explanation.definitionFit: To summarise is to state the main points briefly, so the phrase is a fair paraphrase of the verb.

clue.text: Get going having demolished a meal

indicators.note: to demolish something is to knock it down and remove it, so a letter disappears

blocks.note: to launch something is to get it started
the letter taken out

explanation.surface: Someone sets off after polishing off a quick meal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Demolished a meal' reads as eating greedily, but 'a' is the letter knocked out and 'meal' stands alone as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Lunch is the midday meal, so the general category describes a specific example.

clue.text: Barren region with dearths — area's suffering

indicators.note: something suffering is in a damaged state, so the letters are thrown into disorder

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, ignoring the apostrophe

explanation.surface: A dry land suffers from shortages, a fitting picture of drought.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface feels like a geography lesson about scarcity, which disguises that the two words after the dash-free middle are pure letter fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: The world's largest hot desert is the classic example of an arid, lifeless expanse of land.

clue.text: A group of bosses ready to travel?

blocks.note: taken as written
a company's board of directors runs it

explanation.surface: Executives packed and prepared for a business trip.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags a loose definition: passengers who are on the train or ship are set to depart.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone already on a vehicle is in place for the journey, so the definition is an example, hence the question mark.

clue.text: Tower officer is no vegetarian

blocks.note: first meaning: a Yeoman Warder at the Tower of London
second meaning: read literally, someone who consumes meat from cattle

explanation.surface: A guard at the Tower of London turns out to be a meat-lover.
explanation.walkthrough: The ceremonial guards at the Tower of London are traditionally nicknamed after their reputed meat rations; split the word and it describes a carnivore.
explanation.definitionFit: The nickname belongs to the Yeomen Warders, and taken literally it names a person whose diet includes cattle meat.

clue.text: Legendary ship making a river journey

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the standard abbreviation for river
a go can mean a trip or turn, as in travel

explanation.surface: A mythical vessel sailing up a river.
explanation.walkthrough: Jason and the Argonauts sailed in this ship in Greek myth; the wordplay simply strings three small pieces together.
explanation.definitionFit: Jason's vessel in the Golden Fleece myth is the best-known ship of Greek legend.

clue.text: Some splendid artificial flower in Devon

indicators.note: only some of the following text is used, a run of letters inside it

blocks.note: the run spanning the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A gorgeous fake bloom spotted in a West Country county.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' is crossword shorthand for a river, something that flows; Devon is a county in south-west England through which this river runs.
explanation.definitionFit: A river is something that flows, so it is a flow-er in crosswords; this one runs through Dartmoor to Dartmouth.

clue.text: Coachmen transported American people

indicators.note: transported means carried off or moved elsewhere, so the letters change places

blocks.note: the eight letters used as raw material

explanation.surface: Stagecoach drivers carrying passengers across the American West.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Transported' fits the coachmen story perfectly, which is why it hides as the rearrangement signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The Comanche are a Native American nation of the southern Great Plains, so they are one American people.

clue.text: Food in pub for needy type?

indicators.note: one thing sitting inside another means the outer word wraps it

blocks.note: a bar is a place serving drinks
an example of food

explanation.surface: A pub serving free meals to people in need.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests charity, but the food and the pub are both just pieces; the question mark admits the definition is a loose description.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who begs for money or food is plainly poor and in want, a person in need.

clue.text: Right away I start fights stupidly

indicators.note: acting stupidly means behaving in a muddled way, so the letters come out jumbled

blocks.note: the twelve letters used as raw material

explanation.surface: A hothead confessing to picking fights immediately and foolishly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Right away' sounds like the hothead's speed, but it is the definition, as in love at first sight happening instantly.
explanation.definitionFit: Something happening at the first glance happens immediately, so the idiom matches the adverbial phrase.

clue.text: Material in short letter — broken heart initially exposed in it

indicators.note: something cut short is missing its tail, so the final character goes
something broken is smashed apart, so its letters are rearranged
initially means at the start, so only the opening character is kept
placed inside it, meaning the earlier word wraps around what follows

blocks.note: the word cut short by one letter
taken as written before being reshuffled
the opening letter of the word

explanation.surface: A shortened breakup note revealing a broken heart.
explanation.walkthrough: The heartbreak story hides a busy assembly: the word for letter loses its tail, then takes a shuffled heart plus one initial inside it, with 'it' pointing back to that clipped letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Leatherette is imitation leather, a manufactured fabric, so it is a type of material.

clue.text: Handing over a vehicle

blocks.note: first meaning: the legal transfer of property from one owner to another
second meaning: a means of transport

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase reads as giving someone a car, but it holds two separate meanings, one legal and one about transport.
explanation.definitionFit: In law the word names the transfer of property title, and in general use it names any means of carrying people or goods.

clue.text: These leaders could be real idiots

indicators.note: 'could be' says the letters might become something else once rearranged

blocks.note: the ten letters used as raw material

explanation.surface: A jibe that some political leaders are genuine fools.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leaders' suggests politicians, but in British newspapers a leader is the editorial column giving the paper's opinion.
explanation.definitionFit: A newspaper's leading article, stating its official view, is called a leader in British usage.

clue.text: Report of floral tribute for ex-BBC head

indicators.note: a report is something heard, so the word is taken by its sound

blocks.note: a ring of flowers laid in tribute

explanation.surface: News of flowers being laid in memory of a former BBC chief.
explanation.walkthrough: John Reith was the first Director-General of the BBC, Britain's public broadcaster; the Reith Lectures are named after him.
explanation.definitionFit: Lord Reith founded and ran the BBC in its early decades, so he is a former head of it.

clue.text: Munching hay, animal in high-up region

definitions.note: an adjectival phrase describing location, matching the adjective

indicators.note: munching chews food up, so these letters are ground into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A grazing beast chewing hay in mountain country, perhaps a yak.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Munching' is not the animal's action but a sign to chew up both hay and animal together.
explanation.definitionFit: Belonging to the world's highest mountain range describes something located in a lofty region.

clue.text: Ash found on the beach?

blocks.note: surface reading: cinders or a bonfire's remains left on the sand
setter's reading: ash is a tree, so here it is timber washed ashore by the tide

explanation.walkthrough: 'Ash' suggests burnt remains, but it is a kind of tree, and timber carried in by the sea is what the clue describes.
explanation.definitionFit: Timber washed up by waves, possibly from an ash tree, is the general name for seaborne wood on a shore.

clue.text: The religious leader crossing river brings drink containers

indicators.note: to cross something is to go over it and reach the far side, so one part follows the other

blocks.note: taken as written
R is the standard abbreviation for river
the Hebrew prophet who led the Israelites out of Egypt

explanation.surface: A prophet crossing water carries refreshments, a nod to the Exodus.
explanation.walkthrough: The Biblical leader appears after the river letter, having crossed it; the brand-name vacuum flask has become a common noun with this plural.
explanation.definitionFit: A Thermos is a vacuum flask keeping drinks hot or cold, so several are beverage vessels.

clue.text: Pin I have put in to join sides of raft

indicators.note: the sides of something are its edges, so the first and last letters are kept
inserting something to join two parts means it goes between them

blocks.note: the two edge letters of the word
the contraction I've

explanation.surface: A boatbuilder fixing pins to hold the edges of a raft together.
explanation.walkthrough: The joinery surface is apt, but 'sides of raft' supplies only two letters and 'I have' is contracted.
explanation.definitionFit: A rivet is a metal pin or bolt used to fasten plates together, so pin is a near synonym.

clue.text: Peer at one spitting words in church?

blocks.note: a peer is a member of the nobility
someone who spits sprays saliva

explanation.surface: A nobleman glaring at someone who spits out angry words during a service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Peer at' reads as look closely at, but peer is a noble; the split comes one letter later than the enumeration suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: The Our Father, the prayer taught by Jesus, is the best-known text recited by congregations.

clue.text: Pay to get clock, say, put up

indicators.note: in a down entry, raising something upward makes it read from bottom to top

blocks.note: a clock is one example of a timing device

explanation.surface: Paying a workman to hang a clock on the wall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Say' signals that clock is an example of a wider category; 'put up' suggests hanging but here it turns the word upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: To remit money is to send it in payment, especially by post or transfer.

clue.text: Beam when brat is beaten

indicators.note: something beaten is knocked about and battered out of shape

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An unruly child smiling while being punished, an unsettling image.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beam' looks like a smile, but it is a structural girder whose cross-section is shaped like the letter T.
explanation.definitionFit: A T-bar is a metal girder with a T-shaped profile, used as a structural beam in building.

clue.text: Fellow in sparkling entertainment

indicators.note: the letters sit inside the words that follow, spanning their junction

blocks.note: the run spanning the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A man taking part in a dazzling show.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface asks for a performer, but the answer sits across the join of the last two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Gent is a short informal form of gentleman, and fellow is a common word for a man.

clue.text: Run repeatedly to bring last message

indicators.note: doing something repeatedly means doing it again, so the same piece appears twice in a row

blocks.note: in cricket a bye is a run scored when the ball passes the batsman without being hit
the same cricket run used a second time

explanation.surface: A runner dashing back and forth to deliver one final note.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Run' suggests jogging, but in cricket, the bat-and-ball game, a bye is a run scored without the batter touching the ball.
explanation.definitionFit: This childish farewell is said on parting, so it is the final thing spoken before someone leaves.

clue.text: Form of madness, say, associated with sultanate the reverse of excellent

indicators.note: the reverse means the opposite direction, so the letters are written backwards

blocks.note: e.g. means for example
Oman is a sultanate on the Arabian peninsula
A1 means first-rate, with the digit read as the letter I

explanation.surface: A psychiatric observation linking some kind of mania to a Gulf state, in an awkward sentence.
explanation.walkthrough: A1 is a common rating for first class; the digit 1 doubles as the letter I, so the reversed piece ends the word.
explanation.definitionFit: Egomania is an obsessive preoccupation with oneself, so it is described as a type of mental mania.

clue.text: Sailor's container wrapped in poor paper

indicators.note: something wrapped is enclosed by an outer covering, so one piece goes inside another

blocks.note: a rag is a disparaging name for a low-quality newspaper
a tin is a metal container

explanation.surface: A sailor's tin box packed in cheap newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sailor's' looks possessive but the 's is short for is; a rating is a non-commissioned sailor in the Royal Navy.
explanation.definitionFit: In the British navy a rating is an ordinary seaman, not an officer, so it names a kind of sailor.

clue.text: Speaks by street, speaks with hesitation

indicators.note: by means next to, so the two parts sit side by side

blocks.note: ST is the abbreviation for street
to utter is to say aloud

explanation.surface: Someone talking haltingly on the street corner.
explanation.walkthrough: The repeated 'speaks' itself mimics a stammer; the first is wordplay, the second begins the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To stutter is to repeat sounds involuntarily, a halting manner of talking.
